L1_registration.question: Must an individual register a business to sell digital services/products? Simplest legal form?
L1_registration.answer: A sole proprietorship (Einzelunternehmen) must be entered in the commercial register when it operates in a commercial form and annual revenue exceeds CHF 100,000; below that, registration is voluntary. Liberal professions are exempt unless commercially organised. Unregistered sole proprietorships still appear in the UID register. The owner has unlimited personal liability. Self-employed people must also register with the cantonal AHV/OASI compensation office (not captured).

L4_vat_gst.question: VAT/GST: rate, registration threshold, treatment of exported digital services
L4_vat_gst.answer: VAT is 8.1% (reduced 2.6%; accommodation 3.8%). A Swiss business becomes VAT-liable at CHF 100,000 of turnover from supplies in Switzerland and abroad that are not exempt without credit — worldwide turnover counts, including exports. Services to foreign customers are generally not subject to Swiss VAT (place-of-supply rules, not captured).

L5_data_protection.question: Data-protection law applicable to a small online business
L5_data_protection.answer: The revised Federal Act on Data Protection (nFADP/revDSG) has applied since 1 September 2023, with no transition period, overseen by the Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner (FDPIC). Duties include extended information obligations, information on automated individual decisions, data-subject access and portability, documentation, and reporting data breaches to the FDPIC as soon as possible. A DPO is recommended, not mandatory. TRAP for sole traders: fines of up to CHF 250,000 are criminal sanctions on the responsible individual (e.g. for breaching information, access or cooperation duties), not administrative fines on the company. Only in exceptional cases up to CHF 50,000 can the company itself be fined.

W1_workarounds.question: Simple, legal routes around payment barriers for a beginner (no misrepresentation, nominees or sanctions evasion)
W1_workarounds.answer: Barriers: none of the major platform barriers apply. Simple legal routes: (1) Sell digital products or software through a merchant of record: Paddle (software/SaaS only; each seller reviewed), Lemon Squeezy (bank payouts), Polar, Dodo Payments. The platform is the legal seller to your customers, handles card payments and consumer VAT/sales tax, and pays you out. You still declare the payouts as your income at home (see L3). (2) Sell services on Upwork, which is available here (not on its restricted list). Which withdrawal methods you get (bank, PayPal, Payoneer, etc.) depends on the country and shows in your account. (3) Creator income through the YouTube Partner Program (available here). (4) Paid apps and in-app sales through Google Play (merchant registration available here). (5) Physical or digital goods on Etsy (Etsy seller payments are available here). (6) Client payments by PayPal (on PayPal's Payouts list as 'Fully localized'). (7) Stripe accepts merchants here, so you can take card payments directly on your own site. (8) For direct clients, a bank transfer (SWIFT) into your own local account always works. Follow the local foreign-exchange rules (see P1) and keep invoices. Avoid: opening accounts with a foreign address, a relative's or friend's identity, or a VPN to look like you are elsewhere. It breaches platform terms (accounts and funds get frozen) and can break anti-money-laundering or sanctions law.
